concept.title: Tables
concept.shortdesc: XML has no table element, so your stylesheet decides which elements are a table, its rows and its cells. This chapter explains how to build a table from your elements, how to size it, how to draw its borders and how it breaks across pages. The tables reference at the end lists the properties and display values.

conbody.p: A table in the PDF is a grid of cells. Every element that you want in the grid gets a display value that says what part of a table it is. The element names do not matter: a table element, a list of item elements or any other structure of your XML can be a table.

image.alt: A table drawn as a grid of three columns and four rows. Above it is the caption. The first row is the header group, the next two rows are in a row group, and the last row is the footer group. Each box of the grid is a cell.

conbody.p: These are the display values that make a table:

row.entry: The table. It is a block, like a paragraph.
A table that sits on a line of text, like a word.
The rows that go first and last, and that can repeat on every page.
A group of rows, such as the body of the table.
A cell. It holds the content of the table.
A description of columns, to give them a width, a border or a background. They hold no content.

conbody.p: You do not need to give a value to every element. CSSMedia adds what is missing. A cell outside a row gets a row around it, text that is directly in a table or in a row gets a cell around it, and rows that are outside a row group are fine. White space between the parts of a table is ignored, so you can indent your XML.

Each cell takes the next free column of its row, and a row that has fewer cells than the table has columns is completed with empty cells. CSS gives a cell no span: a stylesheet cannot make one cell cover two columns or two rows.
